generatedDescriptions.description: There's a weight behind your sternum like a hand pressing flat against bone — not painful, but immovable, the kind of heaviness that roots your feet to wherever they are standing. Your attention collapses to a single narrow channel: who is exposed right now, who has their back turned, who doesn't know what's coming — and time compresses until there is only this moment and what you do inside it. Something in you is already moving forward, already positioning between them and the door, before you've decided anything at all.

A cold prickling rises at the back of your neck, settling into a low static hum across your shoulders — not pain, but a tautness, as though your skin has become a membrane reading the air for pressure changes. Your attention snaps to the gap between what someone is offering and what they haven't explained, the too-smooth surface of a gesture that should have rough edges, and time thickens into something granular where you can feel each beat of silence between their words, each micro-pause where a motive could be hiding. There is a pull to step laterally — not away, not yet — but to a vantage point where you can see the whole shape of what's being presented, the way you learned to watch doorways from the side rather than stand framed in the centre of them.

A hot density floods your chest and forearms, like blood rushing to armor plate — your shoulders square without thought and your jaw sets into something that doesn't feel like anger but sits in the same place. Your awareness snaps to the space between someone and the thing bearing down on them, measuring distance and angle as if the geometry matters more than anything anyone is saying. Time doesn't slow so much as clarify — each second arrives with sharp edges, stripped of everything that isn't the gap you could step into, and your body already knows the cost and has decided it's acceptable.

These are the experiences that made you who you are.

**Age 10:** A man in a clean suit came to the neighbourhood offering 'jobs.' Half the kids went with him. Two didn't come back for weeks. Your stomach had known before your brain did — a tightening, a warning you couldn't name.

**Age 12:** Someone tried to take your friend's shoes. He was smaller than you. You took the beating. Afterward, your ribs ached. Your friend said 'You didn't have to do that.' You said nothing.

**Age 15:** A new kid tried to join the group. Friendly, helpful, always around. Your neck prickled every time he laughed too easily. Three weeks later he stole from the stash and disappeared. Everyone was shocked.

**Age 14:** The boss said 'family.' He said it the way people say things they want you to believe. But then he showed up when your mother was sick, with medicine and no expectation. No deal, no debt.

**Age 8:** Growing up on the streets, there was an older kid who shared his food with you. Not because he had to — because he chose to. When he got sick, you sat outside his door all night. Not because anyone asked. Because leaving felt like something breaking inside you. In the morning he said 'You're still here?' and you said 'Where else would I be?' You meant it.

You learned to read people the hard way. The ones who share when they don't have to — those are the ones worth dying for. The ones who smile too easily, who are helpful before you've earned it — your gut tightens. You've been right before about both kinds. Loyalty isn't a word to you. It's the thing that keeps you sitting outside a door all night. But trust? Trust is earned in blood and medicine, not in promises.
You worry about the people you love. When they're out of sight, something in you tightens. You need to know they're safe.
